rv.q: This is a timely and essential revival.
Its power endures: tough, tender and devastating.
Kramer’s play is living history, written without the benefit of hindsight, and it remains undimmed by time.
This production is stripped back and stark.
It is a burning nugget of recent history, a story of people trying frantically to fight back from the brink of annihilation.
As a play it falls too easily into speechifying, especially in an overlong second half.

It is the greatest tribute I can pay to Cooke's new production in the Olivier in the round that he makes its depiction of the early years of the AIDS crisis seem just as raw and horrifying as ever, while drawing from it larger more universal resonances, about love, and politics and society's reaction to disease.
The Normal Heart documents a drama of desperation but it isn’t about doom and gloom; it is about taking action.
The songs are fine, though perhaps not hugely memorable.
If you see one play this autumn, make it this one.
The production demonstrates that, unlike many plays that have become monuments, this one still speaks to our own time with undiminished power and uneasy complexity.
This is not just a play, it’s an event.
The acting is as good as it could possibly be and the relationships are beautifully observed.
The Normal Heart is painfully powerful.

cn.t: Kramer's seminal AIDS drama remains painfully powerful and resonant in Cooke's moving National Theatre revival, anchored by Daniels' compelling performance, though some find the second half overlong and prone to speechifying.
